message:
A northwest jet brings moisture and strong winds to the Northern Mountains Friday night through Saturday. The most snow is expected from 5am to 5pm Saturday, with the highest totals in the Park Range and decreasing as you move south and east. Current models show a wide spread of the upper-end totals, but confidence is high that there will be snow, and strong west and northwest winds will blow it around.

The increase in danger is directly proportionate to the amount of snow that accumulates. In the Park Range, where there is higher confidence of over 1.5 inches of Snow Water Equivalent(SWE) and the potential for two feet of snow, the danger is bumped to HIGH (4 of 5). Here, we expect winds to form thick slabs and rapidly load slopes in the alpine. Our zones at CONSIDERABLE (3 of 5) are expected to get over an inch of SWE and our area at MODERATE (2 of 5) is slated to get over .5 inches SWE. The Storm Slab or Wind Slab avalanche problem is mainly related to slopes that previously had connected coverage of weak old snow. Regardless of where you are in the Northern Mountains, these areas are generally at higher elevations and on slopes facing northwest to north through east. We anticipate that new slabs developing on old faceted snow will react to human pressure and natural loading. The size and distribution of these avalanches will increase in areas set to pick up higher snow totals.

No matter where you travel, this storm marks one of the first large snowfall events of the season for the Northern Mountains. While snow coverage is shallow in many places, it is also weak, and this storm will pack enough punch to build slabs over this weak snow. Listen to signs of instability and adjust your travel plans accordingly. With strong winds and high precipitation rates, anticipate some natural avalanche activity and give steep slopes overhead a buffer. Expect larger avalanches where winds rapidly load lee slopes near ridgelines.

Images.caption: The north-facing slopes of Red Peak from Hoosier Pass on November 12. This is one of the snowier areas in the Northern Mountains right now. Areas with more consistent snow coverage will have a wider distribution of avalanches leading into this storm.
Weak grains like this depth hoar found at Guanella Pass make up the most concerning surfaces as snow accumulates and drifts throughout the day Saturday.
Images.altText: Close-up of angular, translucent faceted ice crystals arranged in three vertical clusters on a black surface.

Images.caption: Strong winds are good at rapidly loading lee slopes and forming thicker and stiffer slabs. These thick slabs are most often found just below ridgelines and on the edges of gullies. These are good areas to avoid as avalanche danger increases. This picture was taken last week when new snow and strong winds caused an uptick in avalanches in the Sawatch Range.

message:
The latest weather model runs agree that we're in for a windy weekend in the mountains. They also agree that the bulk of precipitation associated with this storm will be focused in the Northern and Central Colorado Mountains. We may see an inch or two of snow in the Northern reaches of the San Juan Mountains. Even though we won't receive much new precipitation, there is plenty of snow on the ground that is available for transport. Keep an eye out for newly drifted snow above and near treeline.

The Persistent Slab avalanche problem still exists on previously wind-drifted slopes above 11,000 feet on the north half of the compass. Southern Mountain's observers reported 32 avalanches in the past week, including 17 that were human-triggered. Our Avalanche Explorer shows the pattern well. Of note, many of these avalanches were triggered remotely or sympathetically. The problem is well documented, and has an easy solution: steer around steep slopes below ridgelines and seek out wind-sheltered terrain.

Images.caption: Following strong winds and modest snowfall on November 17th, we saw our first rash of human-triggered Persistent Slab avalanches. Some were remotely-triggered, and one caught a skier. Saturday, November 22nd, brought another wave of human-triggered avalanches following a modest load of new snowfall. Our persistent slab avalanche problem is here to stay for the time being and will require patience to manage.
Look closely and you'll see a crown on the shady shoulder of Treasure Mountain. This avalanche was remote-triggered.
A cornice failure triggered this natural Persistent Slab avalanche on 11/26/

message:
A winter storm arrives early on Saturday under a northwest flow and should bring around 6 to 8 inches of new snow to favored parts of the Central Mountains by Saturday night, including the Elk Mountains and the northern Sawatch Range from Independence Pass through Holy Cross Wilderness. The Grand Mesa and southern Sawatch, as well as southern parts of the West Elk Wilderness only, will see about a trace to maybe 2 or 3 inches of snow by Saturday afternoon. You can expect strong westerly winds with some extreme gusts throughout the duration of the storm at ridgelines, moving a notable amount of snow onto the leeward sides of ridgelines.

As snow starts stacking up, and winds drift additional snow onto leeward slopes, the most concerning slopes will be northeast- and east-facing slopes near and above treeline, where there is already a concerning slab over a weak-layer structure that has proven itself with 55 avalanches on east and northeast aspects near and above treeline in the last week in just the Central Mountains. Slopes below treeline generally lack a persistent weak layer, largely due to early-season rain events melting all the snow below about 10,500 feet, but you can expect the danger to dramatically increase as you climb from around 10,000 feet to about 11,000 feet.

You will most likely see obvious signs of instability as you move to north-facing slopes at these upper elevations if you are breaking trail in an untouched snowpack. That includes collapses and cracking in the snow as you travel across it. If you start to see these signs, it is a clear warning that you should avoid traveling on or under slopes steeper than about 30 degrees that could produce an avalanche large enough to bury you. It is a holiday weekend too, so pay attention to other parties nearby and communicate with each other. We are all very happy to go play in some very welcome new snow, and conditions are very enjoyable at upper elevations right now, but we are also dealing with a dangerous snowpack in some areas, so don’t let your excitement cloud your better judgment.

Images.caption: This avalanche was triggered from around 300 feet away on a northeast-facing slope near treeline in Yule Creek, between Marble and Crested Butte on Saturday, November 21, 2026.
Images.altText: Looking across a snowy slope at an avalanche.

Images.caption: This natural avalanche is a good example of terrain to avoid. Steep, shady slopes below a wind-loaded ridge.

Images.caption: This recent natural avalanche is a good example of where the lingering Persistent Avalanche problem lives, and terrain you should avoid. Notice the snow plume on the ridge. This is a good indication of wind-loading and a slab below.
